summary: A November 12th, 2023 panel convened by the Local Health and Wellness center discussed how long-term social media use affects adolescent mental health. Experts covered the benefits (identity exploration, community, empowerment) and the risks (anxiety, depression, cyberbullying, disruption of developmental tasks). They stressed the roles of parents and schools, resilience-building, and an open debate over regulation of social media companies.
one_line: A Local Health and Wellness panel weighed social media's benefits and mental health risks for adolescents, and the roles of parents, schools, and policy.
key_facts: On November 12th, 2023, the Local Health and Wellness center convened a panel of mental health experts on the effects of long-term social media use on adolescents' psychological wellbeing.
A study released September 15, 2023 by the Adolescent Digital Wellbeing Institute (ADWI) found 95% of teenagers have access to a smartphone.
The ADWI study found over 45% of teens report being online 'almost constantly'.
The ADWI study noted an increase in mental health issues among teenagers, correlated with time spent on social media; depression and anxiety were top concerns.
The ADWI report indicated about 35% of teens have experienced some form of cyberbullying.
Dr. Emily Torres, a clinical psychologist, said social media gives young people a space to explore identities, connect, and express themselves, but warned of unique challenges.
Dr. Torres said adolescents are vulnerable to curated realities that lead to unrealistic standards of beauty, success, and lifestyle, causing inadequacy and low self-esteem.
Timothy Zhang, an educational technologist, said many adolescents find support and information through online communities they may not have access to locally.
Johnathan Reed, a school counselor, said both bullied teens and the bullies themselves face higher risk of depression, anxiety, and even suicidal ideation.
Reed suggested schools incorporate social media and digital literacy into the curriculum and offer school-based programs on recognizing and countering cyberbullying.
Dr. Lara Philips, a developmental psychologist, said screen-mediated communication can undercut conversation, conflict resolution, and deep connection skills.

Dr. Torres recommended open dialogue, setting boundaries, and practicing digital literacy and self-regulation; Dr. Philips recommended mindfulness, physical exercise, offline hobbies, and in-person connections.
The note says debate continues over how much responsibility social media companies should bear and how much regulation is needed.
